title: Orville Peck Dedicates Performance to ‘All the Gay Cowboys’: ‘We Exist, We Walk Among You’
description: Orville Peck made his headlining debut at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night. But it wasn’t the first time the country singer performed at the legen
body:
Orville Peck made his headlining debut at the Hollywood Bowl on Friday night. But it wasn’t the first time the country singer performed at the legendary amphitheater.

	He performed at the outdoor venue during Willie Nelson’s 90th birthday celebration in 2023.

	About a year later, Peck, who is openly gay, and Nelson duetted on a cover of “Cowboys Are Frequently Secretly Fond of Each Other,” Latin country musician Ned Sublette’s 1981 song about same-sex love and lust among the boots and saddles set. The Nelson collaboration is featured on Peck’s 2024 duets album “Stampede.”
	

	“It’s a song that’s very pertinent to my interests,” Peck said, inspiring cheers and applause from the audience. “It’s about gay cowboys. I don’t know if you notice, but I’m a gay cowboy.”


	He continued, “We exist. We walk among you. There’s probably some here. I think I see a bunch.”

	Raising an arm into the air, Peck said, “Let’s dedicate this one to the incredible, incredible Mr. Willie Nelson. I’m sure he’s enjoying an edible somewhere.”

	Before launching into the song, Peck said, “This is for all the gay cowboys.”


	The song includes Nelson crooning, “And I believe to my soul that inside every man there’s the feminine/And inside every lady there’s a deep manly voice loud and clear/And a cowboy may brag about things that he’s done with his women/But the ones who brag loudest are the ones that are most likely queer.”

	The two sing together, “Cowboys are frequently secretly fond of each other/What do you think all them saddles and boots was about?/And there’s many a cowboy who don’t understand the way that he feels for his brother/And inside every cowboy there’s a lady that’d love to slip out.”
	

	A music video for the track was filmed on Nelson’s Luke Ranch in Spicewood, Texas.

	The concert also included a surprise appearance by Noah Cyrus, who joined Peck on stage to duet on “Atchafalaya.” A music video for Peck and Cyrus’ “How Far Will We Take It?” featured a pre-“Heated Rivalry” François Arnaud in a love-triangle storyline.

	During his encore, Peck covered Dolly Parton’s “I Will Always Love You.” Opening acts included Lucius and Deloyd Elze.

	Friday also marked the release of Peck’s fourth studio album, “Mule.” The album chronicles his battle with addiction before getting sober in 2023.

	“These are very deep wounds,” Peck told me during an interview on Wednesday. “What better therapy is there than getting up and being able to express these songs? Then there are people listening and relating, and they’re sharing their pain. It’s a spiritual experience.”

	In the song, “Ring the Bell,” Peck sings of kissing an unidentified pro football “Raiders player.”

	“I did receive permission to sing that lyric from the subject in question, and he was very thrilled,” Peck said. “I told him, ‘Look, I’m gonna keep it sort of ambiguous and mysterious, but I would like to include this in this song.’ He was very, very honored.”

	He added, “I would never have done it if it were somebody who was hiding or fearful of it coming out. This person would have probably allowed me to say their name if I wanted, but I didn’t think it was necessary. People can use their own common sense and discovery to try to figure out who it may be, but that’s all I’ll say.”

schema.headline: Orville Peck Dedicates Performance to ‘All the Gay Cowboys’: ‘We Exist, We Walk Among You’

title: ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Cole Sprouse Heads Up a Hyper-Online Gonzo Freakout in Japan
description: Eugene Kotlyarenko has built a career on drawing upon his widely-viewed cinephilic base of knowledge to consider more contemporary forms of hyper-on
body:
Eugene Kotlyarenko has built a career on drawing upon his widely-viewed cinephilic base of knowledge to consider more contemporary forms of hyper-online, of-the-moment provocation, and “Vintage Violence” is no exception. As with Kotlyarenko’s arguably best-known film, 2020’s “Spree,” live-streaming is key: “Vintage Violence” introduces obnoxious social media celebrity Carter (Cole Sprouse) mid-stream before quickly spinning out into a gangsters-vs-everybody-and-each-other free-for-all. Zipping around Tokyo, Kotlyarenko underlines the of-the-moment-ness of his scenario at every turn, but the film is a surprisingly slow ride despite the overload.
	

	Per his press kit bio, Kotlyarenko specializes in films “exploring love and cultural madness in the age of social media,” of which “Vintage Violence” is definitely one. Carter’s jam-packed introduction finds him in vertical vision while chat-box commenters provide both random insults and background information about the character at a speed almost impossible to process; more relevant details are being dispensed than can possibly be fully absorbed. 


	The impressive density of this overload, which embraces the possibilities of relatively new technology to find novel ways to deliver and compress context, diminishes as Carter is drawn to Japan by Izumi Adachi (Kiko Mizuhara). She lures him with promises of fabulously large sums to be made by selling the vintage denim he found mid-stream — i.e., a duffel-bag-sized Macguffin that can set the protagonists in perpetual motion. (The denim was also apparently integral to the making of the production: per the end credits, “This film was made with the generous support of Levi’s and Levi’s Japan.”)
	

	There is no meaningful trace of the past beyond fetishizable commodities in Kotlyarenko’s film, only the relentless present; shooting with his characteristically tilt-and-zoom-heavy fluidity, cinematographer Sean Price Williams amplifies that twitchy energy.

	Appropriated from a John Cale album, the title accurately describes scenes of bloodletting committed by bizarre, scenery-chewing yakuza members, and the energy hovers somewhere around a bloodier-than-baseline Takashi Miike movie from the mid-2000s. But, per his conceptual preference, Kotlyarenko’s riff on familiar territory is texturally very now, and the setpieces are often based around tech that didn’t exist 20 years ago. The best of these is a chase where Carter’s phone is stolen and he chases down the thief, gauging his proximity by how much his bluetooth earbuds start crackling; the closer he gets, the more unbroken the sound.

	Kotlyarenko is cinematically omnivorous: Beyond the copious Japanese filmmakers he references, “Vintage Violence” riffs on everything from “North by Northwest” to “Wanderlust.” As the plot progresses, increasingly outré elements are introduced: a hotel that seems to have been founded by the same TV programming team that made content in Olivier Assayas’s “demonlover,” or a gangster whose severed finger has been replaced by a spray bottle of poisonous mist. This kind of non-stop maximalism in the service of cult-movie scenes that scream “clip me and put me online!” can quickly grow old, and while “Vintage Violence” is admirably committed to living up to the mayhem of its forebears, like many of them the cumulative effect is more enervating than energizing.

	The film internalizes potential objections about a foreign director making a film that claims insight into Japanese characters’ interiority, with Carter being ritualistically insulted as a gaijin, or outsider. Sprouse is a serviceable lead, adapting to new forms of mayhem while slowly reaching a form of moral rehabilitation, for which he’s rewarded with a romantic arc. For all its determination to be firmly of the Now and provide midnight-movie crassness, “Vintage Violence’s” constituent parts can be surprisingly stock.

schema.headline: ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Cole Sprouse Heads Up a Hyper-Online Gonzo Freakout in Japan

title: Box Office: Zach Cregger’s ‘Resident Evil’ Scares Up $26 Million on Opening Day
description: With fall right around the corner, movie theater-goers are ready to be spooked — and Sony’s zombie horror “Resident Evil” has arrived at the perfect
body:
With fall right around the corner, movie theater-goers are ready to be spooked — and Sony’s zombie horror “Resident Evil” has arrived at the perfect time.

	“Resident Evil” earned $26.3 million domestically across 3,684 screens on opening day, making it far and away the No. 1 new release on Friday. By Sunday, Sony’s new take on the horror franchise is expected to make around $55 million, making it the largest debut in “Resident Evil” franchise history. (2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife,” previously the highest-grossing installment, made $26 million at the box office over its opening weekend.)
	

	Based on Capcom’s popular horror video games, the film was directed by Zach Cregger — who last frightened audiences with 2025’s “Weapons” and 2022’s “Barbarian.” (“Weapons” opened to $43 million and ended its box office run with $270 million globally.) Austin Abrams takes the lead in the gory reboot co-written by Cregger and Shay Hatten as a medical courier who must contend with a zombie outbreak while making a delivery to Raccoon City General Hospital.


	Some die-hard fans were unsure about Cregger’s mission to create a new, original story for the reboot (and thus omit established characters from the “Resident Evil” video game universe), though it seems such concerns were for naught as early reviews and word-of-mouth for the film have been strong. While Variety’s Owen Gleiberman referred to the prior “Resident Evil” films as “hyperviolent, hyperkinetic video-game zombie sludge,” he called Cregger’s take on the IP a “sweetly executed piece of escapist trivia” that has “a quirky relatability.” 
	

	The Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock-led “Practical Magic 2” took second place on Friday, bringing in an additional $3.1 million in its second week. Over the weekend, the witchy sequel is expected to earn another $10.4 million, bringing the film’s cumulative total to $48.2 million.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” both remained in the Friday top 5. Sony’s comic book sequel landed at No. 2, bringing in another $1.53 million, while Universal’s “The Odyssey” took in an additional $ 1.36 million for a fourth-place finish. Those additions bring “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” to a staggering $944.15 million domestic gross, and “The Odyssey” to $609.8 million.

	Vertical’s “The Weight,” another newcomer, pulled in around $1.17 million across 1,504 theaters on Friday, placing it fifth. Per rival estimates, the historical thriller is expected to make $2.3 million through its opening weekend. Director Padraic McKinley’s debut feature stars Ethan Hawke as a battle-scarred veteran hired to smuggle a fortune in gold across 100 miles of impenetrable wilderness. Russell Crowe also stars.

	From GKids, “Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom” opened to $540,000 across 2,173 theaters on Friday, per competitor numbers. The Steve Cox and Matthew Walker-directed animated flick is expected to bring in roughly $1.4 million through the weekend. Per the logline, the film follows Shaun the Sheep (voiced by Justin Fletcher) on Halloween Eve as “excitement turns to dismay when the clumsy Farmer ruins the pumpkin patch. Shaun tries fixing it with science experiments, but things go wrong when a wild beast appears in the woods.”

schema.headline: Box Office: Zach Cregger’s ‘Resident Evil’ Scares Up $26 Million on Opening Day

title: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Sees Mary Embark on Married Life in First Images
description: BritBox have given fans of their hit Jane Austen-inspired series “The Other Bennet Sister” an early Christmas present with a first look at a new thr
body:
BritBox have given fans of their hit Jane Austen-inspired series “The Other Bennet Sister” an early Christmas present with a first look at a new three-part special set to drop this holiday season.

	Ella Bruccoleri returns as the awkward Mary Bennet opposite Dónal Finn as Tom Hayward, who proposed in the Season 1 finale – with Mary accepting.

	“But with marriage comes a new identity and the question remains: who will Mary become as Mrs. Hayward?” reads the logline for the Christmas special.
	

	Returning alongside Bruccoleri and Finn are Ruth Jones as Mrs. Bennet, Tanya Reynolds as Caroline Bingley, Laurie Davidson as Mr. Ryder, Varada Sethu as Ann Baxter, Poppy Gilbert as Lizzie Darcy, Maddie Close as Jane Bingley, Grace Hogg-Robinson as Lydia Wickham, Molly Wright as Kitty Buncock and Anna Fenton-Garvey as Charlotte Collins.


	Joining the cast for the first time is Nerys Amber-Stocks as Mary’s housemaid Lucy.

	“The Other Bennet Sister” is based on Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name. Season 1 was adapted by Sarah Quintrell, who has also written the three-part special based on new storylines by Hadlow.

	Earlier this year, producer Jane Tranter told Variety that while “The Other Bennet Sister” was conceived as a limited series, “the characters just live on.” She said any further seasons “really depends on Janice and her thinking.”

	“At the moment we’re concentrating on looking at the novels of Jane Austen, because that’s what we always set out to do,” Tranter added. “But having set up ‘The Other Bennet Sister,’ you can’t help but think ‘What would happen if – ?’ so we’ll see. We’ll see what Janice says, and Sarah, obviously.”
	

	The first season garnered plenty of fans, with Variety‘s reviewer Aramide Tinubu describing the show as “immensely charming and thoughtful.”

	“The Other Bennet Sister” is produced by Bad Wolf for the BBC and BritBox North America. Asim Abbasi returns to direct.

schema.headline: ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Christmas Special Sees Mary Embark on Married Life in First Images

title: Cate Blanchett Tells Audience To Stop Recording Her London Play: ‘It Spoils It for The Next Group of People’
description: Cate Blanchett asked audience members to stop recording her performance in the London play “Electra/Persona” per a video shared on Instagram Friday.
body:
Cate Blanchett asked audience members to stop recording her performance in the London play “Electra/Persona” per a video shared on Instagram Friday. 

	“There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present,” the actress said on stage. “I understand you like filming the curtain call, and it is kind of flattering in a way. But for anyone who is filming the show, please don’t, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much.”
	

	Blanchett stars alongside Nina Hoss in the play, which is written and directed by Benedict Andrews and runs at the National Theatre’s Lyttelton Theatre until Oct. 10. The actresses alternate between the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma each night, depending on a coin toss. “Electra/Persona” combines Sophocles’ Greek tragedy “Electra” and Ingmar Bergman’s 1996 film “Persona.”


	Beginning her professional acting career on stage at the Sydney Theatre Company, Blanchett previously revealed she “never, ever” thought she could work in the film industry.

	“I was resigned, happily, to a career in theater. I didn’t think I was that girl,” she said at the 2025 Rotterdam Film Festival. “There was a sense women had a certain ‘shelf life’ in the film industry and a certain type of women got to parade on the screen and others didn’t.”

	The Oscar-winning actress is set to star alongside Selena Gomez and Michael Fassbender in “The Brutalist” director Brady Corbet’s upcoming film, Variety confirmed earlier this year. Details about the film remain under wraps, but Corbet has teased it will be X-rated and set in the ‘70s.

schema.headline: Cate Blanchett Tells Audience To Stop Recording Her London Play: ‘It Spoils It for The Next Group of People’

title: Spain’s National Film Prize Honoree Carmen Machi: ‘Acting Has Been the Driving Force of My Happiness and Also a Balm for My Darkest Moments’
description: Actor Carmen Machi, best known for her role as Aida in the wildly popular Spanish series “7 Lives” and spin-off “Aida” as well as her pivotal roles
body:
Actor Carmen Machi, best known for her role as Aida in the wildly popular Spanish series “7 Lives” and spin-off “Aida” as well as her pivotal roles in Almodóvar classics “Talk to Her” and “Broken Embraces,” received the 2026 National Film Prize at the San Sebastian Festival, a prestigious honor that has been granted to a bevy of Spanish greats, including Oscar winners and nominees Penélope Cruz, Javier Bardem, Antonio Banderas, director Fernando Trueba (“Belle Epoque”) and El Deseo producer Esther Garcia, among many others since the Spanish Ministry of Culture launched it in 1980.
	

	The award, presented by the Institute of Cinematography and Audiovisual Arts (ICAA), an agency under the Ministry of Culture, comes with a €30,000 ($34,437) prize.


	In remarks before Machi came up to accept her award, Diego San José, the co-screenwriter of Spanish blockbuster “Spanish Affair” (“8 apellidos vascos”) in which Machi also starred, quipped: “I would say that Carmen is already part of our national heritage, like an aqueduct or like the Burgos Cathedral, but much better preserved than those two examples

	“Besides, Carmen has something that neither an aqueduct nor a cathedral has, and that is that when we look at you, we see ourselves. Today, Carmen, as you go up to collect this award, you carry inside you all those women you have portrayed from the beginning: Your mother, your aunts and your neighbors accompany you.”

	Machi also starred in “Celeste,” created by San José, which won her best actress as well as best series at Series Mania’s International Panorama last year. Superb in Carlota Pereda’s Sundance hit “Piggy,” Machi has demonstrated her chops for drama and melodrama, incarnating the oldest version of a heinously messianic mother in “La Mesías,” from Javier Ambrossi and Javirr Calvo, now behind “La Bola Negra.”  
	

	Spanish Minister of Culture Ernest Urtasun said that he had rarely received so many messages of delight when the ministry announced in June that the award would go to “a truly great actress of innate talent and extraordinary versatility,” whom he compared with such figures as Anna Magnani, the late Marisa Paredes and Julieta Serrano.

	Said Machi: “I’ve always been fascinated by cinema,” relating how her bedroom was filled with clippings and stills of Marlon Brando and how she would hide behind the sofa at the black-and-white movies her parents were watching, and how, struck by a scene, she would run alone to her room and try to recreate scenes in front of the mirror, trying to feel what the protagonist felt, often ending up in tears.

	“It was something that fascinated me. It gave me a strange sense of freedom. I was just a little girl. Then I would leave the room and go back to waiting. I never imagined that that game, which was a refuge to overcome my insecurity and my shyness, would become my craft and my way of life,” she confessed.

	“This profession has given me a wonderful life. It is and has been the driving force of my happiness and also a balm for my darkest moments.”

	John Hopewell contrinuted to this article.



	

					Carmen Machi 
									Carmen Machi  Credit: Caterina Barjau

title: ‘Resident Evil’ Star Austin Abrams on His ‘Tragic’ Transformation, ‘Not Trying to Look Cool’ While Screaming and the One Scene He Wasn’t Allowed to Shoot
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters.

	There’s not a moment in “Resident Evil” where st
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “Resident Evil,” now playing in theaters.

	There’s not a moment in “Resident Evil” where star Austin Abrams isn’t making you laugh, scream or feel bad for the zombie-infested nightmare his character Bryan finds himself in. For almost the entire 95-minute runtime, he’s either running, shooting or getting covered in gore from various undead monsters, like a rat-filled behemoth, a roly-poly ball of bodies or an acid-puking fiend. After teaming with director Zach Cregger on last year’s horror hit “Weapons,” Abrams takes center stage in “Resident Evil” and proves he’s more than capable of leading a feature on his own.
	

	Based on the popular horror video game series, “Resident Evil” tells a fully original story with some nods to the original source material that fans will love. Abrams plays a bumbling medical courier who finds out his girlfriend is pregnant, but agrees to one last delivery before heading home. He must make his way to a hospital in Raccoon City (which is ground zero for the zombie outbreak in the games) to drop off a mysterious package, but the snowy drive is far from easy. Almost immediately, he hits a strange woman with his car, then buckles her in and starts driving her to the hospital without realizing she’s slowly turning into a zombie. They get pulled over by a cop and things quickly go awry. Bryan is able to escape to a nearby farmhouse, but the woman doesn’t stop pursuing him for the entire movie.


	Bryan finds a shotgun at the farm to defend himself, but he realizes the undead creatures will stop at nothing to kill him. After blasting apart the woman and an infected farmer, their bodies fuse together with stringy tendrils from inside each of them. Bryan books it out of there and gets picked up by some scientists from the Umbrella Corporation (an evil institution from the games) who explain that the package he’s delivering contains an antidote to the zombie virus. 
	

	Along the way, Bryan gets bit by a zombie but hides the wound, which slowly infects him. As his condition worsens, he makes it to the Raccoon City hospital, but he doesn’t get the chance to use the antidote. He transforms into a gigantic, tentacled monstrosity in the Umbrella Corporation lab and rips apart the scientists trying to save the world. With their bodies fused to his own, the monstrous Bryan roars atop the hospital as a military helicopter takes aim at him.

	With Variety, Abrams discusses how he transformed into the monster, the cold and messy shooting conditions he endured and the one scene the “Resident Evil” team couldn’t allow him to film.



	

									©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	How did you find the right sound for Bryan’s scream? You really go all out, and it’s played for laughs but also works for a horror movie. Is it similar to your real scream?

	There wasn’t a method behind that. It’s just letting all inhibitions down and not trying to look or sound cool and just letting it come out. I can’t tell you that it was weeks of labored work trying to figure it out. I don’t know the last time a scream naturally came out, so I’m not really sure. Whatever it is is what felt right, especially in the moment for the character. It was something where you didn’t know what was gonna what come out. You don’t want to know. It’s better to just like feel it and let whatever happens happen.

	If Bryan isn’t screaming then he’s usually muttering “fuck!” under his breath. Are you muttering or talking to yourself like that in real life?

	I don’t know if I can say I’m muttering “fuck, fuck” all the time. It was relatively easy thinking about the situation that you’re in at the time. In my daily life, god, that would mean something was really wrong if you did that all the time in your regular life. Those are signs that things are not going well. Please, if that’s happening, something needs to change.

	I was not expecting you to turn into a monster at the end of the movie. What was your first reaction to reading that surprising moment in the script?

	That’s what I love about Zach’s work. He’s willing to take those risks and kill off the person that you’re following the whole time — and not just that, have them ruin everything that they were just fighting for. It definitely was surprising, and also tragic. Everything that this character went through, the change that he has, how he feels with his girlfriend and all this sacrifice is essentially for nothing. It tells the story of why this virus got out and continued to go out and that there was this possibility of it being fixed. I think it’s a cool origin story.
	

	How much of your monster form was practical vs. CGI and other special effects?

	A lot of it was capturing it. It would be hard to build a suit like that. It was kind of a mixture. It’s definitely me, and there’s definitely some stuff they put on my face. I don’t know how they would add all the other different people on me and stuff like that. I don’t know what they fully keep as you or not. But we definitely went through the actions of it.

	What kind of direction was Cregger giving you during the monster fight at the end? What was going through your head?

	What’s going through your head is I look like a fucking idiot right now. It’s so funny because the thing with all that stuff is you can feel dumb, but the less you commit to it, the dumber you look. So actually, the more you commit to it, the more people are just like, “Whoa, that looks cool.” But you know, “More monster.” He would say that a lot. “More roar. Scarier. Monster more. Keep monstering. Don’t stop monstering. Come on, imagine you’re a big, scary monster.” I don’t know, I’m fucking making shit up right now. It was fun. I can’t remember specific notes. A lot of it was just playing around in in this open space and imagining stuff.

	The movie ends with Bryan facing off against a military helicopter. Do you have an idea of what happens to him after? Is that something you’d want to see explored in another movie?

	I don’t know. I’m not sure. I really don’t know. Whatever you want, you want it to be best for the story, and I love Zach. But beyond that, I just don’t know. I don’t want to put in some sort of theories about things.

	The other big part of the movie is Bryan’s relationship with his pregnant girlfriend Michelle, who we never see in person. Who voiced her, and did you ever meet in person or was it just a voice on the phone?

	I think that’s Zach’s wife Sara [Paxton]. We had someone else at the time. She wasn’t where we were shooting at the time, so it’d be too hard to try to patch a call and then it drops out and gets unreliable. We had someone else reading it, but I think he knew he wanted to put Sara in as a fun kind of Easter egg.

	Did you create any more backstory for his and Michele’s relationship than what we see in the movie?

	Yeah, to some degree. There was a coming up with that just for myself, but I don’t know how deeply Zach and I went into it at the time. But it’s something that you need to know to make a full person that feels like there’s dimensions behind what you’re seeing.
	

	How cold was it shooting in Prague?

	Everyday is kind of up and down, but there were days where it was definitely quite cold. I don’t mind that stuff though. There were day where it was this kind of rain that would then freeze to your jacket. So then you’d be covered in this outer layer of ice. But I enjoy that stuff. There were some days where we thankfully got real snow, which was pretty awesome, like fully blanketed. The farmhouse stuff is mostly actual snow that was happening. The temperature was also all in Celsius, which I cannot remember. There were a couple days that everyone was particularly having a tough time. But, whatever, man, it’s just temperature.

	How do you push through the cold when you’re shooting and not let it affect you?

	You just feel it. You let it be a part of the thing. But like I said, it’s not really a big deal. It’s just cold. You know who was concerned was the woman in the dress playing the pedestrian. If there’s anyone to be concerned it was her because she had to do scenes where she was having to lay down in the snow. She was really a killer and not complaining and getting it done. If there’s anyone to pat on the back, it’s her because everyone else got to be fully clothed and not in a summer dress.

	The other thing that stood out to me was all the running you do. Did you train at all to be able to run like that in the snow?

	I don’t know if this is the way to do it, but you want the person to not be a runner. I want to see the person struggling with it. So no, there wasn’t a particular kind of running prep because I feel like it’s just more interesting to watch someone that’s out of breath and you’re like, “I don’t know if they can do this.”

	What was the messiest and bloodiest scene you had to shoot?

	Definitely once we got down to the maternity ward stuff. At that point, you’re completely soaked in this blood and this floor that’s completely blood. People were getting taken out constantly or almost going down. At that point in that movie, there’s not a part of me that’s not completely covered in blood and goo.

	How did you shoot the jump down to the ground from the farmhouse?

	That is one of the only ones that we had a stunt team come in and do. Other than that, it felt it was important to do everything. That was one where, well, I don’t know what to say they just wouldn’t let me do it. But our great stunt guy that did it, he didn’t have any wires on him or anything. He just took the fall. I remember him afterwards saying he really hit his tailbone pretty hard.

title: John Wilson on ‘The History of Concrete’ and What’s Wrong With the Documentary Space: ‘People Are Retelling Stories That Have Already Happened’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “The History of Concrete,” now in theaters.

	John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Co
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains minor spoilers for “The History of Concrete,” now in theaters.

	John Wilson’s new documentary “The History of Concrete” is, of course, about the history of concrete. But it’s also about selling a documentary titled “The History of Concrete,” which, it turns out, is almost as hard as concrete.

	It sees the filmmaker, best known for his HBO series “How To,” traveling across the world — to concrete conventions in Las Vegas and New Orleans, to ancient buildings in Italy and to graves in undisclosed locations. But he also documents the Zoom meetings in between, where he pitches the idea to Hollywood executives and tells them the film’s title. Underneath their deep sighs, you can almost hear them mutter: Who wants to watch a movie called “The History of Concrete”?
	

	“I genuinely did want to make the definitive movie about concrete,” Wilson says of the doc, now in theaters via Magnolia Pictures. “I ended up incorporating the meta aspects about a year or so into the process, because I felt like that was becoming a more interesting story. And I wanted to make something that another filmmaker could learn something from, about how things are produced, because that was always a mystery to me growing up.”


	Of course, it’s not all slabs of rock. Wilson finds humanity in the cracks of “The History of Concrete,” letting his camera guide him toward a professional “gum buster,” a grieving local musician and dozens of other fascinating characters. It is perhaps the filmmaker’s most substantial — and heart-forward — work to date.
	



	

					“The History of Concrete” by John Wilson
									John Wilson
	


	
		In the film, as you’re struggling to sell said film, I kept thinking: It’s John Wilson, obviously he’s not going to make a boring movie about concrete!	

	It doesn’t matter. In terms of the money, we were asking for what a Netflix documentary would cost. Our budget ask was also scaled to what “How To” would cost, so I didn’t think we were being that outrageous. The struggle is actually a lot more real than what’s on screen in the film. I just didn’t want to weigh it down with more struggle.

	People laugh when they hear the title, but you laugh knowing that the movie is done. It’s a lot different when someone is asking you directly for money to make this thing that doesn’t exist yet. Would you give your own money to make “The History of Concrete”? Even if it’s me, I don’t know. It’s a strange proposition.

	The documentary space has mutated slightly, and I think people value the wrong things a lot of the time. That’s what I wanted to comment on, in a way.
	
		What are the things people value?	

	People are focused on retelling stories that have already happened — whether it’s a triple homicide or a musician who has gone through all the motions of their career. Certain people with money have a hard time with imagination and this idea of art-making for the sake of it. You need to go through several layers of approval. I didn’t realize how hard it was going to be.
	
		Structurally, the film is similar to “How To.” Was working in the feature-length format freeing or more challenging?	

	It was freeing in that I was able to have more durational subjects — like the 3,100-mile race that takes place over the course of a few months. I don’t know if I would have been able to cover that as substantially in an episode of the show. Same with one of the main characters I spent a lot of time with near the end of the film. I spent a year and a half with him, and I wouldn’t have been able to do that without the elasticity of a feature film. But emotionally, it is a little different than the show, and while superficially it shares a lot of the same qualities, I set out to make something that was much broader in scope and almost felt like a prequel to the show, because it’s kind of the foundation on which the rest of the work was built.
	
	
		The subject of the film is literally our foundation. I found it notable that you chose to explore concrete, a hard topic, in a physical sense, but you can’t help but be led to the softness — the humanity.	

	Yeah, and Jack, the musician I spent a lot of time with, has the softest heart of all. In the world of hard surfaces, he’s got a really soft interior.
	
		How do you view your responsibility to these subjects, specifically him? Do you approach it as a journalist? Do you have an ongoing relationship with him outside of the film?	

	I met him at a liquor store right next to my house, so he’s the kind of person I’d see all the time. So in that case, I treated it as if he’s someone I’m going to see frequently. But also, my friend Francis Carr, who was one of my producers, would mostly correspond with Jack whenever he was going to have a show or something like that. There was a bit of distance — it wasn’t just him and me. I think there’s some value to a certain level of journalistic distance when making something like this, just because I’m dealing with so many people at the same time.
	
		Has he seen the film?	

	I think he saw part of it in the Rockaways. But he was rehearsing, because he was playing the after party next door during the screening, so he couldn’t fully watch it. He’s going to be at one of the premieres at IFC over the weekend.
	
		I expect that one of the most talked-about moments of the film will be the Kim Kardashian scene. You’re at a GQ dinner and filming Dwyane Wade as he gives a toast to Kim, and she’s looking right into your camera. It’s all very unsettling. How uncomfortable was that to film?	

	The discomfort started when I entered the room, and the filming only eased that discomfort. I had just never seen an uninterrupted shot of Kim Kardashian before, and I knew this was going to be the only chance for me to get it. I wasn’t pursuing it, but I thought it was a very rare environment, and there’s something very awkward and strange about these celebrity events. I wanted to capture that somehow by not including any score and just letting the moment play out, so you have a POV of what it’s like to be sitting across from someone like that at dinner.
	
		Did you have any interaction with her at all?	

	No.
	
		So how does that work? Were you nervous about putting her in the film? Do you expect to hear from her?	

	It’s a miracle that this film exists and is being released as is — that’s what I’ll say. It was an event that was being documented by someone else too, an internal magazine film-and-photo team. I have no idea where that kind of stuff ends up, but I know it won’t be treated anywhere near how I would treat it. So I think that’s how the footage is able to be in the movie, because it was an event that was captured by someone else as well. But I don’t know where that material will ever end up.
	
	
		The shot of Tim Robinson got the biggest laugh of the entire film at the screening I was at. Were you expecting that to be such a punchline?	

	No. Originally we did not have Tim at the end of that shot, because we just wanted you to sit with the strangeness of that eye-contact moment I was having with Kim. We ended up putting the Tim thing in just because it performed really well when we showed it to people, and I realized comedically you needed something to pop that tension bubble. I love reveals that someone else has been there the whole time. I showed the film internationally in a couple of places, and that shot was crickets. There are some places in the world that don’t know Tim in the same way people do here — same with Hallmark and Chef Boyardee. They don’t know what that stuff is.
	
		Is there one shot in the movie you’re proudest of?	

	The shot I really liked a lot was when I’m filming the sidewalk and you see my shadow, but then I’m zooming into the sidewalk, and the light changes really dramatically around me, and my shadow just disappears into the sidewalk. It happened randomly, and it felt very poetic in a way that I didn’t really plan. But on top of that, I think my favorite shot is when the tattoo preservation guy asks his dad where Chef Boyardee is buried. The timing of that was just incredible, and how casual he was.
	
		It turned out to be your kicker!	

	I remember trying to figure out what the last shot of the movie should be when I was talking to [producers] Josh [Safdie] and Ronnie [Bronstein] and Eli [Bush]. I was thinking about going to Chef Boyardee’s grave, but we had to have the movie ready in four days, and I didn’t know how I was going to get it. They said, “You have to get that shot,” so I went and shot it by myself on Christmas Eve, which was the day before we locked the movie. So now I know where Chef Boyardee’s grave is.
	
		Wow, that’s fascinating that the final shot was so last-minute.	

	It was because we got into Sundance as I was still filming the movie. But it also kind of ties in with the Christmas theme of it all, even though you would never know I filmed that on Christmas Eve.

title: Miley’s ‘Bass Persuades’ Is Pretty and Passable, but Surprisingly Light on Bass… or Persuasion: Album Review
description: The title track and first single from Miley Cyrus‘ “Bass Persuades” was a classic act of misdirection, we now learn. Released two and a half weeks p
body:
The title track and first single from Miley Cyrus‘ “Bass Persuades” was a classic act of misdirection, we now learn. Released two and a half weeks prior to the album, the song promised a tenth album full of bangers (with an S or Z, take your pick), mildly scolding the young people for not being interested enough in the dance floor — whatsa matter with kids today? — and aiming to redirect them there with a combination of throbbing rhythms and spoken-word instructions loosely borrowed from the catalogs of Madonna and Lady Gaga. For better or worse, it seemed as if Cyrus was going to drop some of her stylistic eccentricities, along with her last name, and deliver a pure club record.
	

	But that was our supposition, not hers, even if borrowing the single’s title for the whole project did seem to make a promise the full record isn’t prepared to deliver on. The new album, which came out Friday sans press previews, opens with “Bass Persuades” being followed by a second number in a faintly similar vein, “Different Religion,” but then it rarely returns to that territory until the 38-minute collection wraps up with its 10th track, a revved-up and unnecessary remix of the title track. What comes in between includes a surprising number of love ballads and a few odd outliers. It’s eclectic, but not “Endless Summer Vacation”-level eclectic. One thing no one will ever remember about it is the album having a surfeit of bass.


	So how about persuasion? It’s a little light on that, too — pleasant, passable and occasionally compelling, but slight, with hooks that never quite reach the peaks you hope for out of a great pop song, and a bit of an “is that all there is?” feeling at the end of its relatively short length. It will be no one’s favorite Miley album, nor anyone’s least favorite. The overall feel is of something enjoyable on its own terms but a little undercooked in almost every regard, as if the star had been in a rush to deliver product to her new label, even as its primarily lovestruck lyrics — some of which are quite good — surely do reflect where the singer is at in her off-screen life. But for those who admired her previous album, the barely year-old “Something Beautiful,” for finding a cool and interesting retro aesthetic and pretty much sticking with it, “Bass Persuades” seems kind of centerless, more like an in-between project meant to mark time between bolder musical statements than any kind of arrival.
	

	The core message of the album seems to be that things are going pretty well — make that extremely well — with fiancée Maxx Morando, who is a writer-producer collaborator on all but two of the tracks. Hearing Miley in a besotted state turns up mixed results. The third track, “Let’s Get Married,” is an abrupt left turn from the two bang-ier numbers that precede it into synthy easy listening/AC flavors, and what it delivers is not worth the whiplash; while it will probably be heard at some weddings to come, there may be a lot of attendees who would be itchy to please skip ahead to the vows.

	Fortunately, that syrupy aside is a low point from which the album fairly quickly recovers. “Orbit,” next up, is just as romantic but one of the collection’s better tracks, as a power ballad — or even just ballad, without so much emphasis on the power — that applies some clever turns of phrase and thought to what could be a tired metaphor. Her significant other is the center of her solar system: “Place a marble on the floor / When you walk in the room, it’ll roll to you” is an image that makes for a lovely mash note.

	The romantic reveries sometimes give way to things sillier and saucier. “Neon Signs” isn’t a particularly memorable tune unto itself, but the increasingly ridiculous spoken interactions between Cyrus and duet partner Andrew Wyatt may put a smile on your face before all is cooed and done. And/or make you cringe, since, as Wyatt murmurs at the end between the pair’s sexy bedroom oohs and aahs, “Some people think I’m creepy, but others think I’m just right.” An album this immersed in relatively straightforward love songs could use this moment of awkward verbal snogging.

	The album’s best song, “Aftermath,” arrives halfway through, and as the one track that really accelerates into something more impassioned, it would have made an ideal climax for the record, if not for one problem: it’s the only sad song on the album, and thus would be a strange way to wrap up an otherwise cheerful collection. Still, it’s good to know that Miley can take a philosophical moment to ponder The End of All Things — including, inherently, her relationship — as a sort of intermission in an album that’s otherwise characterized by romantic buoyancy.

	There is one other dark track on the album, sure to be its most talked-about number — “Innocent Ways,” which has Cyrus singing at length about a sibling, which many listeners will presume to be Noah. “I want better for my sister / She calls me only when it’s late night and she’s high / Her mind is spinning / Eight nights in a row / She’s been in a crisis / She looks just like me when she cries.” There needs to be some form of crisis to offer some dramatic tension in an album that doesn’t have much, so if she has to borrow the angst from a family member, fair enough. Amusingly, Miley seems to resent her sister for wearing a Blondie T-shirt without actually listening to Blondie music. More intriguingly, she sings, “Fall out from the fame / Claim my mother’s maiden name,” suggesting that this is a family that thinks a lot about last names and how to claim or ditch them. Besides just being legitimately lyrically fascinating, “Innocent Ways” is also the album’s most heated banger — and working out deep-rooted sibling issues over the din of the club is a concept we can get behind.
	

	“Snow” ends the album on a sweeter, if relatively inconsequential-feeling, note, and ought to be the record’s closer, but then Miley evidently thought nine is not enough and makes it an even 10 with the remix of the title track no one asked for. Ending with the most obvious form of filler is not the best look, although, as a non-fan of the original track, I could personally appreciate the amphetamine version of the number a little more.

	Maybe the album seems so short because Miley has booked Hollywood Bowl shows themed around it, and those will be awfully short performances if she sticks primarily to these nine numbers, which presumably she won’t. It doesn’t feel like “Bass Persuades” is going to be an Event Album for Cyrus fans; her followers are notorious for finding her records polarizing, to the extent that an album like “Something Beautiful” earns comments calling it either one of her best or one of her weakest — and yet it wouldn’t be surprising if the fan base is unanimous in finding this new one belongs somewhere in the mid-section of any ranking. “Not bad” is probably not the reaction being sought when someone starts afresh in a business part of their career. But say this for her: she’s someone who never makes the same album twice. So if this one is neither overwhelming nor underwhelming but just kind of whelming, it won’t diminish the appetite for what mode she’ll be in come Miley Mach 11.

title: UMass Dartmouth Running Back Killed in Stabbing
description:
UMass Dartmouth
                          Freshman Running Back Fatally Stabbed in Chest
body:
UMass Dartmouth
                          Freshman Running Back Fatally Stabbed in Chest
                          Across Street From Club
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 19, 2026
                            9:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            UMass Dartmouth running back Marvins Antoine has been fatally stabbed after an attack at a fast-food parking lot ... he was only 18 years old.
      
    
            The stabbing -- which saw Marvins suffering wounds to his chest -- took place at a Wendy's parking lot in Providence early Saturday morning ... WJAR initially reported.
      
    
            Marvin was declared dead upon arrival after being brought to a nearby hospital ... WPRI reported.
      

            Meanwhile, one of Marvin's 19-year-old teammates was treated for "non-life-threatening injuries" ... according to WJAR.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The two reportedly had gone to a local nightlife venue across the street from the Wendy's on Friday with other members of the team.
      
    
            Apparently, the club became overcrowded, and they closed their doors to new arrivals ... Providence Police Major David Lapatin said, according to WPRI. It was then that the fatal fight broke out.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A suspect is currently in custody ... according to the UMass Dartmouth Police Department.
      
    
            UMass Dartmouth said in a statement ... "The entire UMass Dartmouth community mourns the loss of Marvins Antoine. We extend our thoughts and prayers to Marvins family and friends during this difficult time."
